+import uuid
+
+from django.db import connection, models, transaction
+from django.db.utils import IntegrityError
+from django.test import TestCase
+
+from .models import JSONCustomEncoderDecoderModel, JSONModel
+
+
+class JSONFieldTests(TestCase):
+
+    def _test_scalar_value(self, value):
+        obj = JSONModel(value=value)
+        # Oracle Database doesn't allow scalar values
+        if connection.vendor == 'oracle':
+            with transaction.atomic():
+                self.assertRaises(IntegrityError, obj.save)
+        else:
+            obj.save()
+            obj = JSONModel.objects.get(id=obj.id)
+            self.assertEqual(obj.value, value)
+
+    def test_bool_value(self):
+        self._test_scalar_value(True)
+        self._test_scalar_value(False)
+
+    def test_int_value(self):
+        self._test_scalar_value(123456)
+
+    def test_float_value(self):
+        self._test_scalar_value(1234.56)
+
+    def test_str_value(self):
+        self._test_scalar_value('A string')
+
+    def test_dict_value(self):
+        value = {'name': 'John', 'age': 20, 'height': 180.3}
+        obj = JSONModel.objects.create(value=value)
+        obj = JSONModel.objects.get(id=obj.id)
+        self.assertEqual(obj.value, value)
+
+    def test_list_value(self):
+        value = ['John', 20, 180.3]
+        obj = JSONModel.objects.create(value=value)
+        obj = JSONModel.objects.get(id=obj.id)
+        self.assertEqual(obj.value, value)
+
+    def test_nested_value(self):
+        value = {
+            'name': 'John',
+            'age': 20,
+            'pets': [
+                {'name': 'Kit', 'type': 'cat', 'age': 2},
+                {'name': 'Max', 'type': 'dog', 'age': 1}
+            ],
+            'courses': [
+                ['A1', 'A2', 'A3'], ['B1', 'B2'], ['C1']
+            ]
+        }
+        obj = JSONModel.objects.create(value=value)
+        obj = JSONModel.objects.get(id=obj.id)
+        self.assertEqual(obj.value, value)
+
+    def _test_mutable_default_value(self, model):
+        errors = model.check(actually_check=True)
+        self.assertEqual(len(errors), 1)
+        self.assertIn('default should not be a mutable object', errors[0].msg)
+
+    def test_dict_default_value(self):
+        class JSONDictDefaultModel(models.Model):
+            value = models.JSONField(default={'foo': 'bar'})
+
+        self._test_mutable_default_value(JSONDictDefaultModel)
+
+    def test_list_default_value(self):
+        class JSONListDefaultModel(models.Model):
+            value = models.JSONField(default=['foo', 'bar', 123])
+
+        self._test_mutable_default_value(JSONListDefaultModel)
+
+    def _test_valid_default_value(self, model):
+        errors = model.check(actually_check=True)
+        self.assertEqual(len(errors), 0)

The module also uses `json.dumps` and `json.loads` to convert JSON values to Python objects and vice versa. I'm pretty sure there's no database magic involved. body:
This check ensures that *all* database backends support the field. Often projects add a second database in DATABASES that's used for just a few models, for example pulling some data from a reporting system. A database router class often routes queries for just those few tables there.

The checks in Django-MySQL are deliberately more lax, and only return an Error if there is *no* connection that supports the current field, for example: https://github.com/adamchainz/django-mysql/blob/master/django_mysql/models/fields/json.py#L69

I think we should adopt the same logic here :)

+=======================================
+How to enable JSON1 extension on SQLite
+=======================================
+
+This document describes how to enable JSON1 extension on Python's
+:py:mod:`sqlite3` library so that :class:`~django.db.models.JSONField`
+can be used. To check if the extension is enabled on your installation, you can
+do a query with one of the functions included in the extension, e.g.
+``JSON()``. For example::
+
+    >>> import sqlite3
+    >>> conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
+    >>> c = conn.cursor()
+    >>> c.execute("SELECT JSON('123');")
+
+If the query doesn't throw any errors, then the JSON1 extension should already
+be enabled. Otherwise, follow the instructions below according to your
+operating system to set it up correctly.
+
+Linux
+=====
+
+On most major Linux distributions, the JSON1 extension is included in their
+SQLite and/or Python packages and enabled by default. If that's not the case on
+your installation, then do the following:
+
+- Download the `SQLite amalgamation <https://www.sqlite.org/download.html>`_,
+  with or without the configuration script.
+- Extract the source code archive and enter the directory of the result.
+- Compile the source code using the ``-DSQLITE_ENABLE_JSON1`` flag to enable
+  the JSON1 extension. For example:
+
+  .. code-block:: console
+
+      gcc -DSQLITE_ENABLE_JSON1 -c -fPIC sqlite3.c
+
+  To enable other extensions, see the
+  `compilation instructions <https://www.sqlite.org/howtocompile.html>`_.
+- Create a shared library. For example:
+
+  .. code-block:: console
+
+      gcc -shared -o libsqlite3.so -fPIC sqlite3.o -ldl -lpthread
+
+- Place the resulting file (``libsqlite3.so``) in a desired directory, e.g.
+  ``/usr/lib/sqlite3/``.
+- Set the ``LD_PRELOAD`` environment variable. For example:
+
+  .. code-block:: console
+
+      export LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/sqlite3/libsqlite3.so
+
+- Now, the JSON1 extension should be ready to be used in Python and Django.
+  Note that environment variables aren't preserved between login sessions, so
+  make sure it's set before you run Django.

+                key_transforms.insert(0, previous.key_name)

+        json_path = compile_json_path(key_transforms)
+        return "COALESCE(JSON_QUERY(%s, '%s'), JSON_VALUE(%s, '%s'))" % ((lhs, json_path) * 2), params

+    def as_postgresql(self, compiler, connection):

+        if len(key_transforms) > 1:
+            return '(%s %s %%s)' % (lhs, self.postgres_nested_operator), params + [key_transforms]
+        try:
+            lookup = int(self.key_name)
+        except ValueError:
+            lookup = self.key_name
+        return '(%s %s %%s)' % (lhs, self.postgres_operator), params + [lookup]

+class KeyTransformTextLookupMixin:
+    """
+    Mixin for combining with a lookup expecting a text lhs from a JSONField
+    key lookup. On PostgreSQL, make use of the ->> operator instead of casting
+    key values to text and performing the lookup on the resulting representation.
+    On MySQL, JSON_UNQUOTE is applied to the lhs.
+    """
+    def __init__(self, key_transform, *args, **kwargs):
+        if not isinstance(key_transform, KeyTransform):
+            raise TypeError(
+                'Transform should be an instance of KeyTransform in order to use this lookup.'
+            )
+        key_text_transform = KeyTextTransform(
+            key_transform.key_name, *key_transform.source_expressions, **key_transform.extra
+        )
+        super().__init__(key_text_transform, *args, **kwargs)
+
+    def process_lhs(self, compiler, connection):
+        lhs, lhs_params = super().process_lhs(compiler, connection)
+        if connection.vendor == 'mysql' and not connection.mysql_is_mariadb:
+            return 'JSON_UNQUOTE(%s)' % lhs, lhs_params
body:
You use `JSON_UNQUOTE` for text transformations on MySQL and for all key transformation on MariaDB, this should be moved to the `mysql.operations.lookup_cast()`:
```python
    def lookup_cast(self, lookup_type, internal_type=None):
        lookup = '%s'
        if internal_type == 'JSONField':
            if self.connection.mysql_is_mariadb or lookup_type in (
                'iexact', 'contains', 'icontains', 'startswith', 'istartswith',
                'endswith', 'iendswith', 'regex', 'iregex',
            ):
                lookup = 'JSON_UNQUOTE(%s)'
        return lookup
```
after that `KeyTransformTextLookupMixin.process_lhs()` can be removed and `KeyTransform.as_mysql()` can be simplified:
```python
def as_mysql(self, compiler, connection):
    lhs, params, key_transforms = self.preprocess_lhs(compiler, connection)
    json_path = compile_json_path(key_transforms)
    return 'JSON_EXTRACT(%s, %%s)' % lhs, params + [json_path]
```

It's possible by using `Value('null')` (or by `RawSQL`) to store the JSON `null` value in the model and then save it to the database. However, when it's retrieved from the database, we call `json.loads('null')` on the value, which will return `None`. body:
I think you are correct: it is tricky and unexpected, but it's what the databases do. The string of `'null'` is turned into a JSON object (with value `null`). When that is loaded from the database, and turned back into a Python object, it's converted to `None`. Which, unfortunately, is what `NULL::JSONB` is also converted to.

I _guess_ we could convert it to `Value('null')` instead, but that's probably going to be even less fun.

Well, JSON has its own `null` type. It is different from the string `'null'`. Please check this:

```
>>> json.dumps({'a': None, 'b': 'null', 'c': 52})
'{"a": null, "b": "null", "c": 52}'
>>> json.loads('{"a": null, "b": "null", "c": 52}')
{'a': None, 'b': 'null', 'c': 52}
```

If the string `null` and `None` would stringify to the same, it would be a real problem IMO.
https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20160325-the-names-that-break-computer-systems

This check means that **all** of the database connections must support `JSONField` if `JSONField` is used. The previous implementation allows that **at least one** connection supports it. Is this an intended change?
Yes, all connections on which you want to create this model must support `JSONField`'s.

Ah, I didn't catch the `router` part. I've never used it before, but if I'm correct, it should be the better option since it actually checks whether the model will actually be created on the specific connection. Cool!

> Well, JSON has its own `null` type. It is different from the string `'null'`. Please check this:
> 
> ```
> >>> json.dumps({'a': None, 'b': 'null', 'c': 52})
> '{"a": null, "b": "null", "c": 52}'
> >>> json.loads('{"a": null, "b": "null", "c": 52}')
> {'a': None, 'b': 'null', 'c': 52}
> ```
> 
> If the string `null` and `None` would stringify to the same, it would be a real problem IMO.
> https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20160325-the-names-that-break-computer-systems

Actually, we're talking about the possibility of storing the `null` primitive on the field itself. So, it's not something like `{"a": null}`, but just `null`. Those cases you mention are already handled correctly (we actually also use `json.dumps` and `json.loads`).

Normally, Django stores Python `None` as SQL `NULL`. However, since we can store JSON primitives on `JSONField`s, we're wondering how we should handle the `null` primitive. Hope that clears it up @mbeijen!
